books.title: This Is a Bird
books.art_why: Real birds exist today, so photographs can show their beaks and feathers.

pages.text: This is a bird. All birds have feathers, and all birds have beaks. But all birds are different, too.
pages.brief: A single bird stands in a simple natural setting, its feathers and beak clearly visible. The bird is shown from a side angle so both the covering of feathers and the hard beak can be seen. The background stays plain and uncluttered, keeping all attention on the bird itself.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and sharp, and its feathers are black and white. It is an emperor penguin.
pages.brief: An emperor penguin stands upright in a clean, simple outdoor space. Its long, sharp beak points forward, and its black-and-white feathers cover its body. The penguin faces the viewer, with no other animals or objects nearby, so the beak and feather pattern are easy to see.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and hooked, and its feathers are white. It is a pelican.
pages.brief: A pelican stands in a plain outdoor setting, its long, hooked beak held forward. White feathers cover its body. The pelican is shown clearly from the side, with its beak and feathers in full view. The background is simple and empty, with no other animals or objects around.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is sharp and hooked, and its feathers are black. It is a turkey vulture.
pages.brief: A turkey vulture stands in a simple outdoor space, its sharp, hooked beak visible. Black feathers cover its body. The vulture faces slightly to the side so the hooked shape of the beak and the dark feathers are both clear. The background stays plain, with no other animals or objects.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is short and sharp, and its feathers are white. It is a chicken.
pages.brief: A chicken stands in a clean, simple setting, its short, sharp beak pointed forward. White feathers cover its body. The chicken is shown from a clear angle so the short beak and white feathers are easy to see. The background is plain and uncluttered, with no other animals or objects.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and flat, and its feathers are brown. It is a mallard duck.
pages.brief: A mallard duck stands in a simple outdoor space, its long, flat beak held forward. Brown feathers cover its body. The duck is shown clearly from the side so the flat shape of the beak and the brown feathers are both visible. The background is plain, with no other animals or objects nearby.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and curved, and its feathers are brown. It is a thrasher.
pages.brief: A thrasher stands in a clean, simple outdoor setting, its long, curved beak visible. Brown feathers cover its body. The bird is shown from a clear side angle so the curved beak and brown feathers are easy to see. The background stays plain and empty, with no other animals or objects.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is short and sharp, and its feathers are red. It is a cardinal.
pages.brief: A cardinal stands in a simple outdoor space, its short, sharp beak pointed forward. Red feathers cover its body. The cardinal is shown clearly so the short beak and bright red feathers are both visible. The background is plain and uncluttered, with no other animals or objects around.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and thin, and its feathers are purple, green, and gray. It is a Costa’s hummingbird.
pages.brief: A Costa’s hummingbird stands in a clean, simple setting, its long, thin beak held forward. Purple, green, and gray feathers cover its body. The hummingbird is shown clearly so the thin beak and mixed feather colors are easy to see. The background is plain, with no other animals or objects.

pages.text: In some ways, all birds are the same. All birds have beaks, and all birds have feathers. But all birds are different, too.
pages.brief: Several birds stand together in a simple natural setting, each with a visible beak and feathers. Their beak shapes and feather colors differ from one another, showing that all birds share beaks and feathers but are also different. The background is plain and uncluttered, with no people or other objects.

books.title: What in the World Is That?
books.art_why: The platypus and its real body features can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: At the end of this book is a very strange animal. Can you guess what it is?
pages.brief: A very strange animal waits as the mystery subject at the end of the book, with its identity kept back in the scene so young readers can look closely and guess what it might be.

pages.text: It has webbed feet to help it swim. It has a short claw on each toe. Is it a penguin?
pages.brief: A clear close view shows webbed feet with a short claw on each toe paddling through water to help the animal swim, and the scene asks young readers whether this creature could be a penguin.

pages.text: No. It doesn’t have a white belly. If it’s not a penguin, what is it?
pages.brief: The mystery animal is shown without a white belly, so it is clearly not a penguin; with the penguin idea set aside, the young viewer is still invited to keep guessing what it is instead.

pages.text: Its long, flat tail helps it move through water. It lives in rivers, lakes, and ponds. Is it a beaver?
pages.brief: A long, flat tail sweeps through river, lake, and pond water, helping the swimming animal move through these watery places; the scene raises the clear question for young readers of whether it is a beaver.

pages.text: No. It doesn’t gnaw on trees. If it’s not a beaver, what is it?
pages.brief: The mystery animal is shown not gnawing on trees, so it is not a beaver; with that beaver idea ruled out, the young viewer is still left really wondering what the creature could be.

pages.text: It lays small, round eggs. It has a wide bill for getting food. Is it a duck?
pages.brief: Small, round eggs are shown resting together nearby while a wide bill reaches for food in a simple view, and the scene asks young readers clearly whether this animal could be a duck once more.

pages.text: No. It doesn’t quack or have feathers. If it’s not a duck, what is it?
pages.brief: The mystery animal is shown without feathers and does not quack, so it is clearly not a duck; with the duck idea set aside, the young viewer keeps guessing what it really is now.

pages.text: It has thick, shiny fur. Its long, sleek body helps it swim fast. Is it an otter?
pages.brief: Thick, shiny fur covers a long, sleek body as it swims quickly and fast through the water in a clear view, and the scene asks young readers whether this animal is really an otter now.

pages.text: No. It doesn’t have whiskers. If it’s not an otter, what is it?
pages.brief: The mystery animal is shown without whiskers, so it is clearly not an otter; with the otter idea ruled out now, the young viewer is still left wondering what the creature could really be.

pages.text: It’s a platypus! What in the world is that?
pages.brief: A platypus is revealed at last, with its unusual body in clear view, answering the mystery of the strange animal; the final question asks young readers what in the world this creature really is now.

books.title: Stars and Stripes
books.art_why: The book shows colonial times and early flag changes, before photographs could record them.

pages.text: Our flag has a story. The thirteen colonies that formed our country all had different flags.
pages.brief: Several different early colonial flags, each with its own design, are displayed side by side outdoors above a simple row of colonial settlements in the past, showing that the thirteen colonies did not yet share one flag.

pages.text: We needed one flag for all of the United States. We made a flag that had thirteen bright stars and thirteen bold stripes.
pages.brief: A single early United States flag with thirteen bright stars and thirteen bold stripes hangs from a wooden flagpole outdoors under a clear sky, standing alone to show the new flag made for all the states.

pages.text: Our country grew so We made our new flag we added two new stars in red, white, and blue. and two new stripes. We called our flag A famous song was written the Stars and Stripes. about this flag.
pages.brief: A new red, white, and blue United States flag with two added stars and two added stripes hangs from a flagpole outdoors, while soft musical notes drift nearby to show a famous song was written about this flag.

pages.text: Our country grew more We went back to having and more. thirteen stripes on the flag. We needed to change our The stripes show our country flag again. began with thirteen states.
pages.brief: A United States flag with thirteen bold stripes and a cluster of stars hangs from a flagpole outdoors under an open sky, standing for the flag after the country grew and went back to thirteen stripes.

pages.text: We added a star for each new state that joined our country. The star pattern changed as their numbers grew.
pages.brief: Several versions of the United States flag hang side by side outdoors, each with a different star pattern and more stars than the one before, showing a star added for each new state that joined the country.

pages.text: Now our flag has fifty stars for our fifty states. Will there be another star added someday?
pages.brief: The current United States flag with fifty stars and thirteen stripes flies from a flagpole outdoors under a clear sky, with open space around it that suggests the question of another star being added someday.

pages.text: June 14th is Flag Day. We fly our stars and stripes on Flag Day.
pages.brief: People outdoors in a simple setting fly the stars and stripes flag on Flag Day, June 14th, with the red, white, and blue flag waving from a flagpole while they take part in the day.

pages.text: We remember the story of our flag. It is a story that hasn’t ended yet!
pages.brief: A group of people stand together outdoors under an open sky, looking up at the United States flag as it waves overhead, remembering the flag's story and suggesting that the story has not ended yet.

books.title: All Kinds of Homes
books.art_why: Homes are real places that exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Where Do People Live? People live in homes. Not all homes are the same. Homes can be big or small. They can be made of different things.
pages.brief: People are shown living in several homes together. Some homes are large and some are small. The homes are built from different materials. People are inside or near their own homes, in a neighborhood setting.

pages.text: Houses A house is one kind of home. It stands on its own. It has its own roof and front door.
pages.brief: A single house stands on its own. It has its own roof and a front door. The house is separate from other buildings. It sits in a clear spot where its roof and door can be seen.

pages.text: Apartments Apartments are another kind of home. They have one roof. Neighbors live on other floors.
pages.brief: An apartment building has one roof. Apartments are inside it. Neighbors live on other floors. The building shows several floors, with people living in different apartments under the same roof. The neighbors are at home on their floors.

pages.text: Cabins A cabin is another kind of home. It has trees and birds as neighbors. It can be made of logs.
pages.brief: A cabin sits among trees. Birds are nearby as neighbors. The cabin is made of logs, and its log walls are visible. Trees and birds surround the cabin, which stands in a wooded place. It is a home.

pages.text: Motor Homes A motor home is another kind of home. It has wheels. It can move from place to place.
pages.brief: A motor home has wheels. It is a home that can move from place to place. The motor home is shown with its wheels on the ground, ready to travel. It is a home on the move.

pages.text: Houseboats A houseboat is another kind of home. It floats on water. It has fish and other boats as neighbors.
pages.brief: A houseboat floats on water. It is a home on the water. Fish and other boats are its neighbors. The houseboat sits on the water with fish below and other boats nearby. It is a floating home.

pages.text: Special Homes These homes are not like any others. They may be in a unique place. They may not look like homes you have seen.
pages.brief: Special homes are shown in unique places. They do not look like ordinary homes. Each one is different from the others. The special homes may be in unusual settings, and their shapes are unlike homes people have seen.

pages.text: Conclusion Homes can be the same in some ways. Homes can also be different in many ways.
pages.brief: Homes are shown together. Some homes look the same in some ways. Some homes look different in many ways. The picture shows a variety of homes, with sameness and difference both visible. They are all homes.

pages.text: Some homes are very different. Which home would you like to live in?
pages.brief: Several very different homes are shown side by side. Each home looks unlike the others. The homes are all places where people could live. The picture invites a choice among the different homes. They are a mix.

books.title: Caring for Your Dog
books.art_why: Real dogs, families and pet care all exist today, so photographs suit every page.

pages.text: A dog is part of your family. Adding a new dog to your family takes time and special care.
pages.brief: A medium-sized dog sits on the floor of a family living room, close to a parent and a child who are settling in with it. A food bowl and a soft blanket are nearby on the rug, showing the new dog has just joined the household and is being cared for.

pages.text: Choosing a new dog is lots of fun. Choose a dog that fits in with your family.
pages.brief: A family stands together looking at several dogs of different sizes and breeds, one small and one large, as they decide which dog suits their home. A child crouches to meet one dog face to face while the adults watch, all of them calm and happy.

pages.text: Does your family spend lots of active time outdoors? Does your family stay at home or like to travel?
pages.brief: Split scene: on one side a family walks and runs outdoors with their dog on a sunny path; on the other side the same dog rests indoors beside a suitcase, showing that some families stay home and some like to travel.

pages.text: Your family should know all of the things your dog needs. Every dog needs a place to run and play.
pages.brief: A dog runs freely across a grassy backyard with a fence, ears up and tail out, while a child watches from the edge of the lawn. The open space shows the dog has room to run and play safely at home.

pages.text: Your dog needs to be fed twice a day. Your dog needs water all day long.
pages.brief: Two bowls sit on a kitchen floor: one filled with dog food and one filled with fresh water. A dog stands with its head down eating, and a full water bowl stays beside it, showing the dog is fed twice a day and has water all day.

pages.text: Walking is important for your dog’s health. Your dog needs to be walked twice a day.
pages.brief: A person holds a leash and walks a dog along a neighbourhood footpath, the dog trotting beside them with its head up. Trees and houses line the street, showing one of the dog's two daily walks for health.

pages.text: Your dog needs to be played with. You can give your dog treats if he or she is good.
pages.brief: A child kneels on the floor playing with a dog, holding out a small treat while the dog sits and waits politely. A toy lies between them on the rug, showing the dog is played with and rewarded when it behaves well.

pages.text: Your dog needs to be brushed and washed.
pages.brief: A dog stands patiently while a person brushes its coat with a grooming brush. Beside them is a washing tub with water and a towel, ready for the dog's bath, showing the dog is brushed and washed to stay clean.

pages.text: Your dog needs a warm place to sleep.
pages.brief: A dog curls up asleep in a soft bed with a blanket, indoors near a wall, its eyes closed and body relaxed. The warm, cushioned bed shows the dog has a cosy warm place of its own to sleep each night.

pages.text: Most of all, your dog needs a family and lots of love!
pages.brief: A child hugs a dog on the living room floor while other family members sit close around them, all smiling at the dog. The dog's tail is relaxed and its head rests against the child, showing the family and lots of love it needs.

books.title: The Spider's Web
books.art_why: A spider building and using its web is a real, everyday sight in nature today, so real photographs work best.

pages.text: The spider needs to build a new web. The web will help her catch her food.
pages.brief: A spider standing on a twig or leaf, looking out at an empty space between garden branches, ready to begin a brand-new web to catch her food.

pages.text: She chooses a branch to start on. She spins out a thread of sticky silk.
pages.brief: Close view of the spider on a branch, her body tilted as a thin line of shiny sticky silk comes out of her and stretches away from her.

pages.text: She sticks the silk to the branch below. She sticks more silk threads between the two branches.
pages.brief: The spider on a branch with the first silk thread fastened to the branch below her, and more threads running between the two branches.

pages.text: She crawls around and around, spinning silk. She makes many circles to make the web strong.
pages.brief: The spider crawling in circles around her web, pulling silk behind her, the round web shape growing bigger and stronger with each loop.

pages.text: Soon, her web is done. The spider waits quietly.
pages.brief: The finished round web strung between two branches, the spider sitting still at the edge or centre, waiting quietly with her legs drawn in.

pages.text: A fly gets stuck in the threads of the web.
pages.brief: A fly caught in the threads of the web, its wings and legs held by the sticky silk, the spider nearby on the web.

pages.text: The spider creeps toward the fly.
pages.brief: The spider moving slowly and carefully across her web toward the stuck fly, her legs close to the silk threads.

pages.text: The spider bites the fly.
pages.brief: The spider right beside the fly on the web, her mouthparts touching the fly as she bites it.

pages.text: She wraps the fly in silk.
pages.brief: The spider turning the fly over and over, wrapping it round with silk threads until the fly is covered.

pages.text: The spider’s bite changes the fly’s body into goo. When the spider is hungry, she drinks the goo!
pages.brief: The spider at her web with the silk-wrapped fly, drinking the soft goo inside, shown in close-up on the garden web between branches.

books.title: American Symbols
books.art_why: The flag, bald eagle, coins and Statue of Liberty all exist and can be photographed today.

pages.text: Many Symbols The United States has many symbols. A symbol is something that stands for something else. Symbols can be different things.
pages.brief: A wide view of many different symbol shapes gathered together in one scene, each one standing for something else, showing that a symbol can be many different things and that a country can have many of them.

pages.text: American Flag The U.S. flag is an American symbol. It is red, white, and blue.
pages.brief: A United States flag flying outdoors on a flagpole, its red, white, and blue colours clearly visible as it lifts in the air, shown as one of the country's American symbols.

pages.text: The flag has fifty stars. Each star stands for one of the fifty states.
pages.brief: A close view of the blue corner of the United States flag, where fifty white stars are arranged in rows, each single star standing for one of the fifty states.

pages.text: Bald Eagle The bald eagle is an American symbol. It is strong and beautiful.
pages.brief: A bald eagle outdoors with its white head, hooked yellow beak and dark brown body clearly visible, photographed as an American symbol that is strong and beautiful.

pages.text: The bald eagle stands for how strong and beautiful the United States is. You can see the bald eagle on some coins.
pages.brief: Several United States coins lying together, one of them showing a bald eagle, the same strong and beautiful bird that stands for the country, seen close enough for the eagle to be recognised.

pages.text: Statue of Liberty The Statue of Liberty is an American symbol. It is on an island near New York City.
pages.brief: The Statue of Liberty standing on its island near New York City, seen across the water with the city skyline in the distance behind it, shown as an American symbol.

pages.text: The statue has welcomed many people to the United States. It stands for freedom and hope for a better life. The statue was a gift of friendship from France.
pages.brief: The Statue of Liberty with people arriving near it by boat on the water, the statue welcoming them to the United States, standing for freedom and hope for a better life, a gift of friendship from France.

pages.text: Important Ideas The United States has many different symbols. They stand for ideas that are important to people in the United States.
pages.brief: Several different American symbols shown together in one view, the flag, the bald eagle and the Statue of Liberty, standing for ideas that are important to people in the United States.

pages.text: What other U.S. symbols can you think of?
pages.brief: A wide arrangement of several different American symbols with open space around them, inviting the reader to look and think of other United States symbols beyond the ones already shown.

books.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
books.art_why: Leaves, trees, seasons, sunlight, rain, and snow are real-world things that can be photographed.

pages.text: So Many Colors Why are leaves on trees different colors? What makes them change color?
pages.brief: On a tree outdoors, clusters of leaves appear in many different colors. The leaves are attached to branches and fill the view, showing the color differences among leaves on trees.

pages.text: Making Food Leaves make food for the tree from sunlight, water, and air. Green stuff in the leaves helps them make food. It also makes the leaves green.
pages.brief: Leaves on a tree are shown making food from sunlight, water, and air. Sunlight reaches the leaves, water is present, and air moves around them. Green stuff inside the leaves is shown helping make food and giving the leaves their green color.

pages.text: Summer Leaves are green because they are making food. The tree saves some food for winter.
pages.brief: In summer, green leaves on a tree are busy making food. The tree holds onto some of the food to save for winter. The leaves stay green around the branches as the tree prepares for the colder season ahead.

pages.text: Fall In fall, the weather changes. The days get shorter. The nights get longer. Trees get less sunlight, so they make less food.
pages.brief: In fall, the weather changes around a tree. The day is shorter and the night is longer. Less sunlight reaches the leaves, so the tree and its leaves make less food. The scene shows the shift from summer toward fall.

pages.text: The leaves stop making the green color. Other colors that were under the green start to show.
pages.brief: The leaves on the tree stop making the green color. Beneath the green, other colors begin to appear. The green fades on the leaves as those hidden colors start to show through on the tree branches.

pages.text: Leaves turn yellow, orange, brown, and red.
pages.brief: Leaves on the tree turn yellow, orange, brown, and red. The branches hold leaves in these different fall colors, showing the change from green. The leaves hang outdoors on the tree in autumn as the colors spread across them.

pages.text: Winter Trees drop their leaves to get ready for winter. They use the food they saved to get through the cold days and nights.
pages.brief: In winter, a tree drops its leaves to get ready for the cold season. The tree uses the food it saved earlier to get through the cold days and nights. The scene shows the tree in winter without its leaves.

pages.text: Spring Spring comes. Ice and snow melt, and rain falls. The Sun shines. New leaves grow on the trees.
pages.brief: Spring arrives around the tree. Ice and snow melt, and rain falls from the sky. The Sun shines down on the tree. New leaves begin to grow on the trees, showing the change from winter to spring.

pages.text: The green leaves start making food again.
pages.brief: New green leaves on the tree start making food again. The leaves are back on the branches, using sunlight, water, and air as before. The tree returns to its green, food-making state in the new season.

books.title: Wiggly Worms
books.art_why: Earthworms, soil, plants and farmers are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Small Animals, Big Changes Do you know about earthworms? These small animals change the soil in big ways.
pages.brief: A close view of several earthworms wriggling slowly through dark, loose soil. Their small bodies wind between crumbs of dirt, showing how these tiny animals can change the soil around them in big ways.

pages.text: Earthworm Bodies The body of an earthworm is made up of many parts. Each part is shaped like a ring. Each part can bend and stretch. Earthworms move by stretching and pulling their bodies.
pages.brief: A clear close-up view of one earthworm, its long body made of many ring-shaped parts. Each part bends and stretches as the worm moves slowly forward by stretching and pulling its body along the ground.

pages.text: Slimy Worms! Earthworms are slimy. The slime helps keep earthworms cool and wet. It also helps earthworms slide through soil. After worms mate, a ball of slime forms. The slime dries into a cocoon. Baby worms come out of the cocoon.
pages.brief: A slimy earthworm slides through wet soil, its shiny coating keeping it cool and damp. Nearby, two worms have left a ball of slime that dries into a cocoon, with baby worms emerging from it.

pages.text: Earthworm Behavior Earthworms build long tunnels underground. The tunnels keep worms away from heat and sunlight. They also help earthworms hide from hungry animals.
pages.brief: A view below the ground shows several earthworms building long tunnels through the soil. The tunnels keep the worms away from heat and sunlight and help them hide from hungry animals above and around them.

pages.text: Earthworms come out at night to look for food. Some people call them night crawlers. Earthworms eat dead leaves and plants.
pages.brief: At night, earthworms come out onto the ground to look for food. Several night crawlers move slowly among scattered dead leaves and plants, feeding on the fallen plant matter all around them in the dark.

pages.text: Earthworms Are Good for the Soil Farmers love earthworms! Earthworms make space in the soil. The space helps plants get what they need to grow. Earthworm waste helps plants grow big and strong.
pages.brief: A cheerful farmer kneels beside the soil, smiling at several earthworms in the dark dirt. As the worms make small spaces in the soil, their waste helps the nearby plants to grow big and strong.

pages.text: Wanted: Earthworms! Many animals love to eat earthworms.
pages.brief: Several earthworms wriggle close together on the soil while a group of different hungry animals gathers nearby, eager to eat them. The worms look small beside the many animals that love to feed on them.

pages.text: Earthworms are small, but they have a big job. Earthworms help plants grow!
pages.brief: Several small earthworms move quietly through the dark soil beside young green plants. Their bodies are tiny, but their work in the dirt helps the plants grow, showing the big job these little animals do.

books.title: Ride, Cling, Run
books.art_why: All the animals shown are real living species that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Animals Come and Go Many animals travel from place to place. They travel to find food, water, and shelter.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor scene showing several different kinds of animals on the move at once, some walking and some swimming, travelling across open ground and past water toward food, water and shelter in the distance. The animals are spread out across the landscape, clearly going from one place to another.

pages.text: Baby animals often travel with their parents. They may ride, cling, or run with their parents.
pages.brief: A parent animal with its baby close beside it, the young one holding on and staying near as they move forward together across natural ground. The baby keeps close to the parent's body, showing how young animals travel alongside the adults that care for them.

pages.text: Ride Baby lions are called cubs. Some cubs ride in their mother’s mouth. Lions sleep in dens.
pages.brief: A lion mother carrying a small cub gently in her mouth as she walks across dry grassland, with another cub nearby. In the background a shaded den area where lions rest, the family moving toward it under warm open sky.

pages.text: Baby fish hatch from eggs. Some baby fish ride in their father’s mouth. Fish live in water.
pages.brief: Underwater view of tiny baby fish newly hatched from small round eggs, gathered close to an adult fish. One baby fish is held safely inside the father fish's open mouth, while the others swim in the surrounding water among water plants.

pages.text: Cling Baby spiders hatch from eggs. Some baby spiders cling to their mother’s back. Most spiders climb on webs.
pages.brief: A close view of a mother spider with many tiny baby spiders clustered and clinging to her back. Nearby, spiders climb across silken webs stretched between plant stems, the hatchlings holding tightly to the parent as she rests.

pages.text: Baby frogs hatch from eggs. Some baby frogs cling to their father’s back. Frogs can live in water and on land.
pages.brief: A father frog at the edge of a pond with tiny baby frogs clinging to his damp back. Around him the water surface and muddy bank show both the wet and dry places where frogs live, the young ones gripping his skin.

pages.text: Run Baby penguins hatch from eggs. Baby penguins run behind their parents. Penguins like to swim, but they can also run.
pages.brief: Adult penguins moving across cold open ground with baby penguins running closely behind them in a line. Behind the group, icy blue water where penguins swim, showing the birds both on land and in the sea.

pages.text: Baby wolves are called pups. The pups run with their parents. Wolves sleep in dens.
pages.brief: Wolf pups running alongside adult wolves across grassy ground near a rocky den. The pack moves together, the pups keeping pace with the adults, the dark opening of the den visible where the wolves rest and sleep.

pages.text: Ride, Cling, Run Baby opossums are called joeys. First, joeys ride in their mother’s pouch. Then, they cling to their mother’s back. Later, they run from place to place.
pages.brief: A mother opossum with tiny joeys, one riding inside her pouch and another clinging to the fur on her back. Further along the same scene, a young opossum running on its own across the ground, moving from place to place.

books.title: Are You From Australia?
books.art_why: Real Australian animals and places can be photographed.

pages.text: I live in Australia. It is a large country with lots of open space. Many animals live here.
pages.brief: A large, open Australian landscape with wide grassy space and scattered trees under a bright sky. A few native animals are visible far off among the grass and trees, suggesting that many animals live in this country.

pages.text: I live in the rivers of Australia. I look like a beaver with a duck’s bill. I eat tasty bugs on the river bottom.
pages.brief: A platypus swims along the bottom of a clear Australian river. It has a beaver-like body and a duck’s bill. It noses through the riverbed, eating small tasty bugs. Green river plants and smooth stones surround it underwater.

pages.text: I live in the forests of Australia. I am one of the biggest bats in the world. I eat sweet fruit and flowers.
pages.brief: A large fruit bat hangs in a forest tree in Australia, with wide wings folded at its sides. It is one of the biggest bats in the world. Nearby are sweet fruits and bright flowers. It reaches toward a flower and a piece of fruit to eat.

pages.text: I live in the deserts of Australia. I hop on two big legs. I carry my baby in a pouch.
pages.brief: A kangaroo stands in an Australian desert, balancing on two big hind legs. A tiny baby kangaroo peeks out from the pouch on its belly. The mother kangaroo is ready to hop across the dry, open ground under a warm sky.

pages.text: I live in the deserts and forests of Australia. I roll into a ball when I am scared. I eat yummy ants.
pages.brief: An echidna in an Australian desert or forest curls tightly into a ball on the ground, hiding its face and legs. Small ants crawl nearby on the soil and dry leaves. The echidna has rolled up because it is scared, and it eats these yummy ants.

pages.text: I live in the trees of Australia. I make my nest with leaves. I am yellow with a green body.
pages.brief: A small bird with yellow and green feathers perches in an Australian tree. It carries leaves in its beak and adds them to a nest among the branches. Sunlight filters through the green leaves around the bird and its leafy nest.

pages.text: I live on the seashore of Australia. I dig holes in the sand to lay eggs. I catch fish in the sea.
pages.brief: A small penguin stands on an Australian seashore beside a sandy hole it has dug. The sea stretches behind it with small fish swimming in the water. The penguin is preparing to lay eggs in the sand and will catch fish in the sea.

pages.text: I live in the trees of Australia. I eat nothing but special leaves.
pages.brief: A koala sits high in an Australian tree, gripping the branches with its claws. It chews on special leaves, eating nothing else. More leaves grow around it in the green canopy, and the koala looks calm as it feeds among the branches.

pages.text: I live in the waters of Australia. I swim in rivers, lakes, and even the sea.
pages.brief: A sleek water animal swims through Australian waters, moving from a river into a lake and out toward the open sea. Its body cuts through the water, and ripples spread behind it. The scene shows water stretching from inland rivers and lakes to the salty sea.

pages.text: All of these animals are from Australia, and I am from Australia, too!
pages.brief: A group of the Australian animals from the previous pages stands together on open ground: a platypus, a fruit bat, a kangaroo, an echidna, a yellow-and-green bird, a small penguin, a koala, and a water animal. A smiling child stands with them, showing they all come from Australia.

books.title: A Taste for Blood
books.art_why: Every animal shown — leeches, mosquitoes, lampreys, bats, ticks, fleas, lice — exists in the real world today and can be photographed close up.

pages.text: A leech sucks blood from a fish’s eye. All animals need to eat food to live. For some animals, that food is another animal’s blood. A Taste for Blood.
pages.brief: Underwater close view: a leech fastened to a fish's eye, its body pressed to the fish's head as it feeds. The fish's head fills much of the picture, still and close, in dark water.

pages.text: Mosquitoes bite animals to drink their blood. Female mosquitoes drink blood. These small insects leave marks that itch.
pages.brief: A mosquito stands on an animal's skin, mouthparts lowered, drinking blood. Another female mosquito rests nearby on the same animal. The bites leave small marks on the skin that itch.

pages.text: Main photo: A lamprey has gills like other fish. Small photo: A lamprey has many teeth. Some lampreys drink blood. These fish have round mouths full of little teeth. A Taste for Blood.
pages.brief: Two views of a lamprey. In the larger picture its body and gills show, gills like those of other fish. In the smaller picture its round mouth is open, ringed with many little teeth.

pages.text: Top: A vampire bat drinks blood from a cow. Bottom: Vampire bats have sharp teeth. Some bats drink blood. These mammals fly out to feed at night.
pages.brief: Top: a vampire bat clings to a cow and drinks its blood. Bottom: a close view of a vampire bat's face shows its sharp teeth. These bats fly out at night to feed.

pages.text: Main photo: A tick drinks blood from a dog’s face. Small photo: A tick crawls across an animal’s fur. Ticks drink blood. These animals are like spiders. They hide on leaves or grass. They grab onto animals that walk past them. A Taste for Blood.
pages.brief: Main picture: a tick holds onto a dog's face in the fur, drinking blood. Small picture: a tick crawls across an animal's fur. Ticks wait on leaves and grass, then grab animals that walk past.

pages.text: A leech sucks blood from a human leg. Most leeches drink blood. These worms live in marshes, rivers, and ponds.
pages.brief: A leech clings to a human leg, sucking blood from it. The leg is shown close and large in the picture. Most leeches live in marshes, rivers and ponds.

pages.text: A vampire finch bites another bird to drink its blood. One kind of bird drinks blood. These small birds peck at larger birds. A Taste for Blood.
pages.brief: A vampire finch perches on a larger bird and pecks at it, biting to drink its blood. The small bird leans in toward the bigger bird, feathers close together in the frame.

pages.text: Top: A bedbug can live for more than one year without eating. Bottom: A bedbug crawls across a human thumb. Bedbugs drink blood. These insects hide in and around beds.
pages.brief: Top: a bedbug shown alone, a creature that can live more than one year without eating. Bottom: a bedbug crawls across a human thumb, its small flat body tiny against the skin.

pages.text: Main photo: A flea jumps over a cat’s body. Small photo: A flea has long legs for jumping. Fleas drink blood. These insects can’t fly, but they can jump very far. A Taste for Blood.
pages.brief: Main picture: a flea in mid-jump above a cat's body, legs stretched out. Small picture: a close view of a flea showing the long legs it uses for jumping. Fleas cannot fly.

pages.text: A head louse gets caught on the teeth of a comb. Animals that drink blood have been around for a long time. You don’t want to be their next meal!
pages.brief: A head louse caught on the teeth of a comb, held between them. The small insect sits against the comb in close view, filling the picture, with the comb's teeth around it.

books.title: Living Or Nonliving?
books.art_why: A toy robot, a brown bear, gears and a battery are all real things a camera can show.

pages.text: This toy robot is not. This brown bear is a living thing. and another is not? How can you tell when one thing is living Introduction.
pages.brief: A toy robot and a brown bear shown together, side by side. The robot is a toy, stiff and still, while the bear is a living thing, a real animal with fur, eyes and a body of its own. The pair sets up the question of how you can tell which is living.

pages.text: Living and Nonliving Things Living things are alike in important ways. Living things all grow and make more things like themselves. They also use energy, move, change, and are made of cells.
pages.brief: Living things shown growing bigger, with young ones standing beside older ones of the same kind. Each one moves, changes and uses energy, and each is made of cells. The group makes clear the important ways in which all living things are alike.

pages.text: They are not alike in all the ways, or they They may move, change, or use energy. in some ways. Nonliving things may be like living things would be living things.
pages.brief: A living thing and a nonliving thing placed side by side for comparison. The nonliving one may move, change or use energy in some ways, so it looks a little like a living thing. The two are alike in some ways and different in others.

pages.text: Compare Living and Nonliving Things Some of the ways they are different are easy to spot. The toy robot does not grow.
pages.brief: The toy robot shown again beside a living thing, close enough to compare. The robot stays exactly the same size, its body fixed and unchanging, while the living thing grows. Not growing is one easy difference to spot between the two.

pages.text: It cannot make more things like itself.
pages.brief: The toy robot alone, still and unchanged, with nothing new of its kind appearing beside it. It cannot make more things like itself, while living things do. This is another clear difference that separates the toy from a living thing.

pages.text: Some of the ways they are alike can make it tricky. The toy robot does move and use energy.
pages.brief: The toy robot in motion, wheels or joints turning, showing that it does move and does use energy. Because it moves and uses energy, it shares some features with living things, which is what makes telling living from nonliving tricky.

pages.text: It has gears and a battery that help it move.
pages.brief: A close look inside the toy robot at the gears that turn and the battery that powers it. The gears mesh and the battery feeds them energy, and together they are what help the robot move the way it does.

pages.text: Dead Things Nonliving things are not dead. Dead things were once alive but now are not. Nonliving things were never alive.
pages.brief: A thing that was once alive and is now dead shown beside a nonliving object that was never alive. Dead things were once living but are not now, while nonliving things were never alive at all.

pages.text: Which of these things are living or nonliving? can be fun. Figuring out if something is living or nonliving Conclusion.
pages.brief: A mixed group of things laid out together, some living and some nonliving, waiting to be sorted into two groups. Figuring out which is living and which is nonliving is shown as something enjoyable to do.

books.title: Taking the Train
books.art_why: Trains, tracks, stations, and city scenes are real today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: The horn blows. The train rolls along the track.
pages.brief: A train rolls steadily along a railway track outdoors, moving forward as its horn blows. The engine and passenger cars stretch along the rails in an open setting, showing the train traveling on its way.

pages.text: When the train stops, some people get on. Other people get off.
pages.brief: When the train stops, people get on while other people get off. Some passengers step aboard through the open doors, and other people step down onto the ground, showing the change of passengers at the stop.

pages.text: The train rolls along the track again. It heads toward the big city.
pages.brief: The train rolls along the track again, heading toward the big city. It travels steadily forward across the open landscape, with the big city ahead in the distance as the train continues its long journey.

pages.text: It goes faster as it moves along. Sometimes it races forward. Sometimes it rocks side to side.
pages.brief: The train moves faster along the track. It races quickly forward at speed through the landscape, and at times it rocks side to side as it travels onward, showing the motion of the fast-moving train.

pages.text: Some people read on the train, while others rest. Some people talk to each other, while others talk on their phones.
pages.brief: Inside the train, some people sit and read while others rest. Some people talk quietly to each other, and other seated passengers talk on their phones, showing different ways people spend time on the journey.

pages.text: The train passes grassy fields. It crosses rivers. It passes stores, schools, and backyards.
pages.brief: The train passes wide grassy fields and crosses a river. It moves past nearby stores, schools, and backyards, showing the different places along the route as the train travels steadily through the surrounding area outside.

pages.text: The train enters a long tunnel.
pages.brief: The train enters a long railway tunnel. It moves into the dark tunnel opening in the landscape, with the tunnel stretching ahead as the train passes slowly inside and disappears from the open outside view.

pages.text: The train arrives in the city! Here, tall buildings rise toward the sky.
pages.brief: The train arrives in the city. Many tall buildings rise toward the sky around it on all sides, and the train comes into the busy city street setting with the tall buildings standing high overhead.

pages.text: The train makes one last stop. All the people get off. Other people get on.
pages.brief: The train makes one last stop at the station. All the people get off while other people get on, showing many passengers leaving the train and new passengers stepping aboard at the crowded final stop.

pages.text: Soon the train rolls along the track again. It rolls back through the tunnel. It rolls back past towns and grassy fields. The horn blows.
pages.brief: Soon the train rolls along the track again. It rolls back through the long tunnel and past towns and open grassy fields, with the horn blowing as the train travels onward on its return journey.

books.title: Zoo Data
books.art_why: Real children, animals, and zoo settings can be photographed.

pages.text: Allie, Jo, and Chris are going to the zoo. Did all of the kids find the same information? They will record what they see.
pages.brief: Allie, Jo, and Chris arrive at the zoo together, ready to record what they see. The three kids carry their own materials and look around the zoo, wondering whether they will all find the same information.

pages.text: “I’ll draw a graph,” says Chris. “I’ll use tallies,” says Jo. “I’ll make a table,” says Allie.
pages.brief: Chris, Jo, and Allie stand together at the zoo, each choosing a different way to record information. Chris draws a graph, Jo makes tally marks, and Allie starts a table with her pencil near the animal exhibits.

pages.text: First, the kids see three elephants.
pages.brief: At the zoo, Allie, Jo, and Chris stop to watch three elephants. The elephants stand together in their enclosure while the kids look on and prepare to record what they see with their notebooks ready.

pages.text: Allie starts her table. Elephant How Many Animal Animal Table.
pages.brief: At the zoo, Allie begins her table on a clipboard, starting with the elephant they saw. She holds a pencil and writes her first entry while standing near the elephant area. The table is for the animal count.

pages.text: Next, the kids see two bears.
pages.brief: Next, the kids see two bears at the zoo. Allie, Jo, and Chris watch the two bears in their enclosure, and the kids get ready to add the bears to their records for the next count.

pages.text: Jo marks her tally chart. Bear l l l Elephant Animal Tally Chart.
pages.brief: Jo marks her tally chart with a pencil, adding marks for the bear they saw. Her tally chart includes the bear and elephant groups as she records the animals at the zoo, standing near the bears.

pages.text: Then, the kids see four wolves.
pages.brief: Then, the kids see four wolves at the zoo. Allie, Jo, and Chris watch the four wolves together in their enclosure, and the kids prepare to record the wolves for their animal data with their pencils ready.

pages.text: Chris draws his graph. Wolf Bear Elephant Animal Graph.
pages.brief: Chris draws his graph on paper at the zoo, showing the animal groups they have seen so far. He holds a pencil and adds to his graph while standing near the wolf area with careful marks.

pages.text: Animal Tally Chart Elephant l l l Bear Wolf l l l l Which group has the most animals?
pages.brief: The three kids gather together around Jo's tally chart, studying the groups for elephant, bear, and wolf. They compare the marks and ask which group has the most animals at the zoo during their visit.

pages.text: How many animals are there in all? Wolf 2 Bear Elephant How Many Animal Animal Table.
pages.brief: At the zoo, the kids look over their records and count the animals in all. They compare the wolf, bear, and elephant groups, using Allie's table to help add the groups together for a total.

pages.text: Animal Graph Animal Table.
pages.brief: The kids finish at the zoo, holding Chris's graph and Allie's table side by side. They look over their recorded animal information together, ready to compare what they found and share their results with Jo nearby.

books.title: Squirrel Acrobats
books.art_why: Gray squirrels exist today and can be photographed in nature.

pages.text: Gray squirrels are some of nature’s acrobats. They move quickly and easily to find food or escape from other animals.
pages.brief: Several gray squirrels move quickly and easily through their surroundings as they search for food or escape from other animals. Their quick, sure movements make them look like nature’s acrobats as they move about the area.

pages.text: They dart or dash across the ground. They can stop quickly with their tails up. They are alert for danger. They whip their tails from side to side if they see other animals.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel darts or dashes across the ground and then stops quickly with its tail lifted high. It stays alert for danger, and if it sees other animals, it whips its tail from side to side.

pages.text: They move fast on the ground. They run and leap quickly so that cats or foxes do not catch them.
pages.brief: Gray squirrels move fast on the ground, running and leaping quickly so that cats or foxes do not catch them. One squirrel dashes ahead on open ground, using speed to escape danger.

pages.text: They cling to tree trunks with their claws.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel clings to a tree trunk with its claws, holding tightly to the tree bark. Its body stays pressed close to the tree as it looks around, using its grip to stay in place.

pages.text: They can climb and change direction quickly. They can change direction to escape from birds or other squirrels.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel climbs up a tree trunk and changes direction quickly, twisting and turning easily as it moves around the tree. It uses this quick change to escape from birds or other squirrels nearby.

pages.text: They can leap easily from large branches to small ones.
pages.brief: High in a tree, a gray squirrel leaps easily through the air from a large branch to a small one. Its body stretches out as it makes the jump, showing how it moves from branch to branch.

pages.text: They land easily on small branches by using their tails. They use their tails to keep their balance and not fall off.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel lands easily on a small branch and uses its tail to keep its balance. As it settles, its tail helps it stay steady on the branch so that it does not fall off.

pages.text: Small branches or wires are like tightropes that they easily run across.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel runs across a small branch or a wire, treating the narrow path like a tightrope. It moves easily along the line, crossing from one side to the other while keeping its balance.

pages.text: They can hang from the bottoms of branches. They can even climb upside down!
pages.brief: A gray squirrel hangs from the bottom of a branch, holding on as its body turns downward. It can even climb upside down, moving along the underside of the branch with its claws and feet.

pages.text: Squirrel acrobats can quickly and easily climb, leap, and run!
pages.brief: Gray squirrels, the acrobats of nature, climb, leap, and run quickly and easily. Their nimble movements carry them through the trees and along the ground, showing their skill as they go from place to place.

books.title: Meet the Beetles
books.art_why: Beetles are real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: Beetles are amazing insects. Like other insects, beetles have three main body parts.
pages.brief: A beetle stands alone in a simple, clear view. Its body is divided into three main body parts, and the head, middle section and rear section are all clearly visible as the beetle rests quietly.

pages.text: Most beetles have two pairs of wings. The front wings are hard and thick to protect the pair underneath.
pages.brief: A beetle is shown with two pairs of wings. The hard, thick front wings are partly lifted, revealing the softer pair underneath. The front wings look strong and protective as the beetle rests in a simple natural setting.

pages.text: All beetles have a hard skeleton on the outside of their bodies. The skeleton protects the beetles.
pages.brief: A close view of a beetle clearly shows the hard skeleton on the outside of its body. The strong outer skeleton covers and protects the beetle as it stands quietly in a simple natural setting.

pages.text: There are many different kinds of beetles. There are more kinds of beetles than any other living thing.
pages.brief: Several different kinds of beetles are shown together in a clear view. Each beetle has a different shape, color and pattern, showing that there are many kinds of beetles, more than any other living thing.

pages.text: Beetles can live almost anywhere. Beetles can live in forests. Beetles can live in deserts.
pages.brief: One beetle is shown in a forest among trees, while another beetle is shown in a desert with sand and dry ground. The two very different places show that beetles can live in forests and deserts.

pages.text: Beetles can live in jungles. Beetles can even live in and around water.
pages.brief: A beetle is shown in a jungle with thick green plants, and another beetle is shown in and around water. The scenes show that beetles can live in jungles and even in and around water.

pages.text: Beetles change several times as they grow. Each time they change, they look very different.
pages.brief: A beetle is shown at different stages as it grows and changes. Each stage looks very different from the others. The changing forms are placed side by side, showing that beetles change several times and look different each time.

pages.text: Beetles eat many different things. Some beetles eat dead plants and animals.
pages.brief: A beetle is shown eating dead plant material, and another beetle is shown eating a dead animal. The scene shows that beetles eat many different things, and some beetles eat dead plants and animals in a natural setting.

pages.text: Some beetles eat animal waste. Some beetles eat plants. Some beetles eat other insects.
pages.brief: Three beetles are shown with different foods in a natural setting. One beetle is near animal waste, one is eating a plant, and one is eating another insect, showing that beetles eat animal waste, plants and other insects.

pages.text: Beetles are amazing insects!
pages.brief: A single beetle is shown in a clear, close view. Its hard wings, outer skeleton and small body are clearly visible as it rests quietly in a simple natural setting, showing a very amazing insect.

books.title: Scorpions
books.art_why: Scorpions are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Scorpions are arachnids. Spiders and ticks are arachnids, too.
pages.brief: A photo shows a scorpion, a spider, and a tick together in one clear view. The scorpion stands in the foreground with claws and tail visible, while the smaller spider and tick are nearby, showing three arachnids grouped together.

pages.text: All arachnids have a hard shell. All arachnids have two body parts and eight legs.
pages.brief: A close-up photo of an arachnid shows its hard outer shell, two body parts, and eight legs. The body is clear and simple, with the legs spread out around it so the two parts and eight legs can be seen plainly.

pages.text: Scorpions also have a pair of claws. Scorpions use their claws to grab prey.
pages.brief: A scorpion uses its pair of claws to grab small prey. Its claws are closed around the prey while the rest of its body stays low, showing how the front claws hold and grip the animal it is catching.

pages.text: Scorpions also have a long tail. At the end of the tail is a stinger. The stinger has venom in it.
pages.brief: A close-up photo shows a scorpion's long tail curving forward, ending in a stinger. The sharp stinger at the tip is shown clearly, and the tail is held up so the stinger and the venom inside it are the focus.

pages.text: Scorpions use their tail to sting animals that try to hurt them. Scorpions use their tail to sting prey, too. Scorpions come out at night to hunt for prey.
pages.brief: At night, a scorpion hunts small prey, its long tail arched forward to sting. Nearby, another animal approaches, and the scorpion turns its stinger toward it in defense. The scene shows the scorpion using its tail both to hunt and to protect itself.

pages.text: Scorpions eat a lot at one time. Scorpions eat a lot of different small animals. Some scorpions eat other scorpions!
pages.brief: A scorpion feeds on a large meal, with several different small animals around it. Another scorpion is nearby as possible prey, showing that some scorpions eat other scorpions and that a scorpion can eat a lot at one time.

pages.text: There are about 1,500 kinds of scorpions. Some scorpions are small. Some scorpions are big.
pages.brief: A photo shows two scorpions together, one much smaller and one much bigger. They are placed side by side in one view, making the size difference clear and showing that scorpions can be small or big.

pages.text: Some scorpions are blue or green. Some scorpions are yellow or red.
pages.brief: Several scorpions are shown in one view with different colors: one blue, one green, one yellow, and one red. Their bodies and claws are clearly visible, showing the range of colors that some scorpions can have.

pages.text: Some scorpions glow in the dark!
pages.brief: In the dark, a scorpion glows with a faint light. Its body, claws, and tail are visible in the darkness, showing that some scorpions glow in the dark and making the glowing scorpion the clear subject of the photo.

books.title: Signs Are Everywhere
books.art_why: Signs, streets and shops exist in the real world today, so real photographs fit best.

pages.text: Signs are everywhere. Signs are on posts. Signs are on buildings.
pages.brief: A sunny street corner where a metal sign is fixed to a tall post on the pavement, and a second flat sign is mounted on the brick wall of a building behind it, both facing the road.

pages.text: Where else do you see signs? They hang above streets. Signs are in windows and on doors.
pages.brief: A city street seen from below, with a long sign hanging above the roadway between two buildings. Nearby, a small sign stands in a shop window and another sign is fixed to a closed door.

pages.text: Signs tell us lots of things. Signs tell us what to do. They tell us when to walk and when not to walk. They tell us when to stop and when to go.
pages.brief: A crossing where a signal sign shows a walking figure and another shows a raised hand. Beside the road, a red stop sign and a green go sign stand on their posts at eye level.

pages.text: What do these signs tell us? and how fast we can go. They tell us how far to go and where not to go. Signs tell us where to go.
pages.brief: A row of roadside signs on posts: a round speed limit sign with a number, a sign showing distance ahead, a sign with a crossed-out arrow, and a sign with an arrow pointing the way to go.

pages.text: Signs give us warnings. They warn us about children playing. They warn us about animals on the road.
pages.brief: Two warning signs on posts beside a road: one shows children running, the other shows a deer standing, set against a hedge and open fields with a road curving past.

pages.text: What do these signs warn us about? They tell us to drive slowly on winding roads.
pages.brief: A yellow warning sign on a post beside a narrow road that bends and winds away between grassy banks, with the curved arrow on the sign echoing the shape of the road ahead.

pages.text: People make signs for lots of things. They make signs for sales. They make signs for lost animals.
pages.brief: A shop window filled with a bright sale sign, and beside it a wooden post with a paper poster showing a lost dog, the paper slightly curled at the corners.

pages.text: What other things do people make signs for? People make signs to advertise things.
pages.brief: A row of large advertising signs on buildings and boards along a busy street, each one bright and colourful, standing above the pavement where passers-by would look up at them.

books.title: Places People Live
books.art_why: The book shows real places and real houses that exist today, so photographs fit best.

pages.text: People live in many different places. They live where it is cold. They live where it is hot.
pages.brief: People are shown living in a cold place, wrapped up against the chill, and in a hot place under bright warmth. Both groups stand outdoors as the scene compares two very different everyday environments where people make their homes.

pages.text: They live where it is wet. They live where it is dry.
pages.brief: People are shown in a wet place, with damp air and rainy ground, and in a dry place with dusty, parched ground. The two scenes sit side by side to show how people live in very different weather.

pages.text: Some people like to live high up. A few people live way high up.
pages.brief: Some people are shown living high up on a hillside or mountain slope, while a few people live much higher still. People stand near their homes as the scene looks upward at homes set far above the surrounding land.

pages.text: Some people even live below the ground. Some people live down low.
pages.brief: Some people are shown living below the ground, in homes set into the earth. Others are shown living down low, close to the ground. The scene contrasts underground homes with low homes in a simple, clear view.

pages.text: People live in many different kinds of houses. They live in houses made of stone. They live in houses made of grass.
pages.brief: People are shown with many different kinds of houses. Some houses are made of stone, with solid walls, and some are made of grass, with natural textures. The scene shows these varied homes side by side.

pages.text: People even live in houses made of ice. They live in houses made of glass. They live in houses made of sticks.
pages.brief: People are shown beside houses made of ice, glass and sticks. One house has clear, glassy walls; another is built from ice blocks; another is made from gathered sticks. The scene presents these unusual homes together.

pages.text: Some people live high above the ground. Some people live deep below the water.
pages.brief: Some people are shown living high above the ground, in homes raised into the air. Other people are shown living deep below the water, in submerged homes. The scene contrasts these two extreme places people call home.

pages.text: Some people build homes in caves or on cliffs. Some people live in the ground.
pages.brief: Some people are shown building homes in caves or on cliffs, with rock surrounding them. Others are shown living in the ground. The scene shows these rough, natural settings in different places where people make their homes.

pages.text: Some people live in houses that move. Some houses are on wheels. And some float on the water.
pages.brief: People are shown with houses that move. One house sits on wheels, like a vehicle home, and another floats on the water. The scene shows both kinds of moving homes and how they can travel.

pages.text: But no matter what it is, a house is a home. They can be made of strange things. They can have strange shapes. Houses can be strange.
pages.brief: A house is shown as a home, no matter what it is made of. Houses with strange shapes and strange materials sit together. The scene presents many odd-looking homes, all still called home, in one view.

books.title: The Food We Eat
books.art_why: real foods, farm animals and crops that exist today photograph naturally

pages.text: There are many kinds of food. Where does food come from? It all comes from plants and animals.
pages.brief: A wide table spread with many different kinds of food — bread, fruit, vegetables, a jug of milk and a plate of meat — with a leafy green plant in a pot at one side and a chicken and a cow standing in a sunny farmyard behind the table.

pages.text: Oranges grow on orange trees. Orange juice comes from oranges. Where does orange juice come from?
pages.brief: A tall orange tree heavy with round orange fruit in a sunny grove, and beside it a glass jug of orange juice with a halved orange on a wooden board, drops of juice running down the side of the glass in the warm light.

pages.text: Where does milk come from? Milk comes from cows. Cows are animals.
pages.brief: A dairy cow standing in a green pasture, black and white markings clear, looking toward the viewer, while a metal pail of white milk sits on the grass in front of her and other cows graze in the background under a soft sky.

pages.text: Wheat grows from Bagels come from wheat. Where do bagels come from? the seeds of a wheat plant.
pages.brief: A field of golden wheat with ripe seed heads bending in the wind, and in the foreground a close view of wheat seeds beside a woven basket holding round bagels, a farmer's hands lifting one bundle of cut stalks.

pages.text: Where do omelets come from? Omelets are made from eggs. Eggs come from chickens.
pages.brief: A farmyard hen standing on straw in a wooden coop with brown eggs resting in the nest behind her, and nearby on a table a folded omelet on a white plate with a fork beside it in morning light.

pages.text: They are really part of the stem part of the potato plant’s root. Most people think potatoes are French fries are made from potatoes. Where do French fries come from? that grows below the ground.
pages.brief: A potato plant with green leaves above dark soil, and below the ground a cutaway showing the round potatoes and their roots and stems, while a basket of golden French fries sits on the grass above the soil.

pages.text: Where does hamburger meat come from? Hamburger meat is made from beef. Beef comes from cattle.
pages.brief: Cattle standing together in an open grassy field, brown and black coats, heads lowered to graze, with a package of ground hamburger meat on a wooden board in the foreground and a fence line running behind the herd.

pages.text: Corn is a seed from a corn plant. Popcorn comes from corn. Where does popcorn come from?
pages.brief: A tall corn plant with green leaves and a ripening ear of corn wrapped in husks, standing in a sunny field, with a striped bowl of popped popcorn resting on a cloth nearby and loose corn seeds scattered on the ground.

pages.text: Where does cheese come from? Cheese is made from milk. Milk comes from cows.
pages.brief: A wedge of pale yellow cheese on a wooden board beside a glass of milk, with a dairy cow grazing in a green meadow behind, and a small churn and cloth on a bench at the edge of the farmyard.

pages.text: Pizza comes from plants and animals. The pepperoni comes from a pig. The cheese is made from milk. The sauce is made from tomatoes. The crust is made from wheat. Where does pizza come from?
pages.brief: A whole pizza on a wooden table, cheese melted and bubbling, slices of pepperoni and red tomato sauce visible, with a wheat stalk, a red tomato, a block of cheese and a pig standing in a pen in the background of the farm scene.

books.title: A Seed Grows
books.art_why: Real seeds, soil, rain and plants exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: A small seed falls to the ground and becomes buried in the soft soil.
pages.brief: A tiny brown seed falls onto soft dark soil in a garden bed and settles into a shallow dip, half-buried by loose crumbs. The ground around it is damp, crumbly and open to the air.

pages.text: The seed is buried in the soft soil, and the rain falls.
pages.brief: The small seed lies buried in soft dark soil. Rain falls steadily from a grey sky onto the garden bed, striking the soil surface. The wet ground darkens, and water begins to sink into the loose earth around the hidden seed.

pages.text: The rain soaks into the soil that holds the small seed.
pages.brief: Rainwater soaks down into the soft soil around the small buried seed. The ground is dark and wet, with tiny droplets clinging to soil crumbs. Below the surface, the seed sits in damp earth as water moves through the spaces between the grains.

pages.text: The small seed soaks up water from the rain.
pages.brief: A close view of the small seed in damp soil shows it taking in water. The seed is swollen and wet, surrounded by dark, moist earth. Water from the rain has soaked the ground, and the seed rests in the wet soil.

pages.text: The water helps the seed, and roots grow down deep into the soil.
pages.brief: The wet seed in soft soil begins to change. A small root pushes downward from the seed, reaching deep into the dark, damp earth. The root is pale and thin, and the soil around it is moist from the rain.

pages.text: The leaves gather in the sunshine. grow up through the ground. The leaves and a stem.
pages.brief: Green leaves and a short stem push up through the soil into open air. The young plant stands in a garden bed, with leaves spread to catch the sunshine. Sunlight falls on the leaves, and loose soil surrounds the base of the stem.

pages.text: The plant uses sunshine to make food. The rain and the soil help the small plant.
pages.brief: The small green plant stands in sunshine in a garden bed. Its leaves are spread wide, and the damp soil around its base is dark from rain. Sunlight falls on the leaves as the plant grows, with water in the soil below.

pages.text: They go deep in the ground. The roots grow longer. and more leaves grow on the stem. The plant grows taller.
pages.brief: The plant is taller now, with a longer stem and more leaves. Its roots reach deeper into the dark soil below. The garden bed is damp, and the stem rises upward with leaves spreading out on both sides.

pages.text: The big plant grows flowers. The flowers make seeds.
pages.brief: The big plant stands tall in the garden bed, with flowers opening on its stem. The flowers are full and open, and seeds are forming inside them. Green leaves and a strong stem support the blooms above the damp soil.

pages.text: What will happen next? A new seed falls into the soft soil.
pages.brief: A new small seed falls into the soft dark soil in a garden bed. It settles into a shallow dip in the ground. The soil is damp and loose around the seed, ready for what comes next.

books.title: Whose Eggs Are These?
books.art_why: Real animals and their eggs exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Many animals lay eggs. Eggs can be strange and beautiful. These eggs are in a nest of twigs and soft grass. They are a beautiful sky blue. Do you know whose eggs these are?
pages.brief: A close view of a nest made of twigs and lined with soft grass. Inside the nest sits a cluster of smooth, sky-blue eggs, all gathered together in the cup of the nest. The eggs are a clear, bright blue against the brown twigs.

pages.text: These are robin eggs.
pages.brief: The sky-blue eggs are shown close up in their nest of twigs and soft grass. They are robin eggs, smooth and pale blue, clustered together in the cup of the nest. The grass lining cradles them.

pages.text: These tiny eggs are on the bottom of a leaf. They can be round like pearls, or they can be spiny. Whose eggs are these?
pages.brief: Tiny eggs cling to the underside of a green leaf. Some are round like small pearls, while others are spiny, arranged together in a little cluster on the leaf's bottom surface. They are very small.

pages.text: They are butterfly eggs.
pages.brief: The tiny eggs on the underside of the leaf are butterfly eggs. They sit in a cluster on the green leaf, small and round, and some have a spiny surface. They cling to the leaf's bottom.

pages.text: There are many eggs in this tiny case. It looks like light brown cotton candy, but it is made of silk. Whose eggs are these?
pages.brief: A small silk case holds many eggs. The case looks like fluffy light brown cotton candy, soft and fibrous, and the tiny eggs are packed inside its silken walls. It is a tiny case, full of eggs.

pages.text: You can find them They are spider eggs. near spider webs.
pages.brief: A cluster of spider eggs sits inside a silky case near a spider web. Thin web threads stretch nearby, and the eggs are gathered together in their silk covering. The web is close to the egg case.

pages.text: These large eggs aren’t in a nest or case. They sit on cold rocks. But feathers help keep them warm. Whose eggs are these?
pages.brief: Large eggs rest on cold, bare rocks instead of in a nest or case. Feathers lie around them, helping to keep the eggs warm on the rocky ground. The rocks look hard and chilly.

pages.text: Penguins keep eggs warm These are penguin eggs. with their feet and feathers.
pages.brief: A penguin stands on cold rocks, keeping large eggs warm on its feet and under its feathers. The eggs rest against the penguin's body, sheltered by its warm covering. The penguin's feet support the eggs.

pages.text: This strange egg floats in the ocean. It is inside a small, tough case. Whose egg could this be?
pages.brief: A single strange egg floats in the ocean. It is enclosed in a small, tough case that drifts in the blue water, bobbing near the surface. The case looks firm and protective around the egg.

pages.text: This is a shark egg.
pages.brief: The floating egg in its small, tough case is a shark egg. The case drifts in the open ocean water, holding the egg inside its firm, protective shape. Blue water surrounds the drifting case.

pages.text: These eggs float on a pond. There are tiny inside each egg. Whose eggs are these?
pages.brief: A cluster of small eggs floats on the surface of a pond. Each egg is round, and something tiny can be seen inside, resting on the calm water. The eggs drift together in a group.

pages.text: The fish-shaped things are tadpoles. They are frog eggs. They are not fish eggs.
pages.brief: Small fish-shaped tadpoles swim in the pond water near the floating eggs. These are frog eggs, not fish eggs, and the tadpoles have rounded heads and wiggling tails. They move through the calm pond water.

books.title: Ants, Ants, and More Ants
books.art_why: Ants are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: You can find them on trees and and dirt in your yard. You can find them in the grass of different places. You can find ants in lots Ants Everywhere! in your home.
pages.brief: Ants crawling on a tree trunk outdoors, ants moving through dirt in a yard, ants in blades of grass in different places, and ants walking across a floor inside a home. Show many ants in each spot so viewers see ants everywhere.

pages.text: What Do Ants Look Like? Ants are insects. Their bodies have three parts, and they have six strong legs.
pages.brief: A close view of one ant standing on the ground. Its body clearly shows three parts, and its six strong legs are visible as it stands. The ant is an insect, shown alone so the three body parts and six legs are easy to see.

pages.text: Ants have two antennae red, green, or yellow. They can be black, brown, Ants can be different colors. that they use to touch and smell.
pages.brief: An ant seen close up, with two antennae raised in front, touching and smelling. Show ants in different colors: black, brown, red, green, and yellow, each standing on the ground with antennae clearly visible.

pages.text: Ants can be tiny or large. Some big ants are as large as a paper clip. Ants are very strong for their size.
pages.brief: Two ants side by side for size: one tiny ant and one large ant. The big ant is as large as a paper clip lying beside it. The large ant stands firmly, showing how very strong ants are for their size.

pages.text: They use their jaws strong jaws. Some ants have large, to cut food and to fight.
pages.brief: An ant using its large, strong jaws to cut a piece of food. Another ant stands ready with its strong jaws open, as if to fight. Show the jaws clearly on each ant as they work and face off on the ground.

pages.text: Groups of Ants Most ants build nests under or on top of the ground.
pages.brief: A group of ants building a nest. Show one nest under the ground, with ants carrying bits of soil, and another nest on top of the ground, with ants gathered around it. The ants work together in a group.

pages.text: The queen ant lays have different jobs. Different ants in the nest all the eggs.
pages.brief: Inside the nest, the queen ant lays eggs while other ants stand nearby. Show the queen with eggs under her, and different ants around the nest doing their own jobs, all in the same underground nest space.

pages.text: Some worker ants take care of the eggs and baby ants. Some worker ants get food. Soldier ants guard the nest.
pages.brief: Worker ants taking care of eggs and baby ants in the nest. Other worker ants carry food. Soldier ants stand at the nest entrance, guarding it. Show the three kinds of work happening at once in and around the nest.

pages.text: You can have fun Ants are amazing animals. Watching Ants watching ants at work.
pages.brief: A person watching ants at work, looking closely as ants move along the ground or a nest. The ants are busy, and the watcher has fun observing them. Show the ants as amazing animals going about their work.

books.title: Animal Eyes
books.art_why: Real animals and their eyes can be photographed today, so photos show them clearly.

pages.text: You use your eyes to see. Animals use their eyes to see, too.
pages.brief: A young child stands looking out with eyes wide open, and nearby animals of different sizes also have their eyes open and facing forward, all of them seeing the world around them in a bright outdoor place.

pages.text: Animal eyes can be small or large. Some animal eyes can look very strange!
pages.brief: A close look at animal eyes of very different sizes: one set tiny and narrow, another set large and round, both filling the frame. Beside them, an animal's eyes have an odd, strange shape and pattern unlike the others.

pages.text: What animal has eyes that look like this?
pages.brief: A close-up view of a pair of animal eyes filling the picture, with round dark centres and a clear pattern around them. Nothing else of the animal is shown, so the eyes are the only thing to look at.

pages.text: This spider does. It has eight eyes that look like little dots. Most spiders can’t see very clearly. But many spiders are very good at seeing things move.
pages.brief: A spider sits on its web with eight small eyes arranged across its head, each one like a tiny dot. The spider is still and faces forward, its dotted eyes clearly visible in the close view.

pages.text: What animal has eyes that look like this?
pages.brief: Two large round animal eyes fill the frame in a close-up view, facing forward, bright and still. Around them only a soft blurred edge is visible, so the eyes themselves are the whole picture.

pages.text: This owl does. Its eyes help it see well at night. An owl cannot move its eyes. It must turn its head to look around.
pages.brief: An owl perches in the dark, its big round eyes facing forward. Its body stays still while its head is turned to the side to look around, because its eyes cannot move in their sockets.

pages.text: What animal has eyes that look like this?
pages.brief: A close-up view of an animal's two eyes sitting high on the head, each one round with a patterned rim, filling the picture. The eyes are the only part shown, held still and facing out.

pages.text: This kind of lizard does. Each eye can look in a different place. The left eye sees one thing. The right eye sees something different at the same time.
pages.brief: A lizard rests on a warm rock, its two eyes set high on its head. One eye looks one way while the other eye points a different way, so the lizard watches two separate places at the same time.

pages.text: What animal has eyes that look like this?
pages.brief: A close-up view of a large animal eye made of many tiny rounded sections packed tightly together, filling the frame. The surface is curved and patterned, and only the eye is shown.

pages.text: This dragonfly has eyes that are made up of many tiny eyes. Dragonflies are very good at seeing things move. Use your eyes to see all the animal eyes around you.
pages.brief: A dragonfly rests on a thin stem, its huge eyes covering most of its head, each eye made up of many tiny eyes. It faces forward in a sunny garden, ready to spot the smallest movement.
